units.translation: which I defended with similar examples in Oxford Annotations p. 85 and Hermann in Annotations p. 113, though these are not very certain, since ὡς [as] could be corrupted from ὧν [of which], which the scribes left untouched in other places. Hence in Aeschylus I wrote μᾶσσον ὧν ἐμοὶ γλυκύ [greater than which is sweet to me], unless Elmsley's very gentle correction μασσό νως ἢ μοί γλυκύ [greater than sweet to me] is to be preferred. Less probable is ἢ ὡς [or as] with synizesis, which Turnebus mentions from some copy.

which the scholiast explains: οὐ τοσοῦτον ἰσχύει εἰπεῖν ἄγγελος ὡς ὁ αὐτόπτης [a messenger is not so able to speak as the eyewitness]. Therefore οὐδὲν ὡς [nothing as] is said with the infinitive like οὐδὲν οἷον [nothing like] with the infinitive, which Blomfield compared, adducing examples from Aristophanes Av. 966 οὐδὲν οἷόν ἐστ᾽ ἀκοῦσαι τῶν ἐπῶν [there is nothing like hearing the words] and Plato Gorg. p. 447 c. οὐδὲν οἷον τὸ αὐτὸν ἐρωτᾶν [there is nothing like asking oneself]. To these Scholefield added Demosth. p. 529 οὐδὲν γὰρ οἷον ἀκούειν αὐτοῦ τοῦ νόμου [for there is nothing like hearing the law itself].
Preceded by οὕτως [thus].
With τώς [thus] answering in the other member of the sentence.
unless ἠκούσαθ᾽ ὧν [you heard of which] is to be written, as at line 46 ὧν [of which] was corrupted into ὡς [as].

where τεύχειν [to make] is used for ἔτευχον [I was making], the infinitive being referred to the parenthesis ὡς ἐγὼ ᾿δόκουν ὁρᾶν [as I seemed to see], of which negligence there is another example in this play at 565 τυτθὰ δ᾽ ἐκφυγεῖν ἄνακτ᾽ αὐτὸν ὡς ἀκούομεν [and we hear that the king himself escaped a little], which I emended by restoring αὐτόπουν [with his own feet]: about which I spoke in Philologus vol. 13 p. 476 477.
Which is also said ὡς τάχος [as quickly as possible] at Sept. 675, Ag. 27, Ch. 889.
where ὢν [being] is more probable, which Wakefield restored.
It is constructed with the indicative in direct speech.
With the indicative of past tense it signifies that we wished something to happen which was in vain.
Much more frequently with the subjunctive, when a present or perfect tense with present meaning precedes.
Thus Emperius and Martin for ἄλλος ἂν εἰδὴ τοῦτ᾽ ἄρ᾽ — [another would know this then —].
which is nothing other than ὡς ἁπλῷ λόγῳ εἰπεῖν [to speak in a simple word].

Different from this is ὡς [as] marked with an accent when it is postponed to the thing compared, as at Sept. 498 βακχᾷ πρὸς ἀλκὴν Θυιὰς ὡς [like a Thyiad for battle], and in other places indicated above.
